comments.author: artrax
comments.text:
We build this as a c++ library, do to query-compilation for our stream processing engine.
https://github.com/nebulastream/nautilus
It allows us to implement operators or functions without having to write them in terms of LLVM IR DSL (or similar). Rather, you write your functions over a wrapper type (and returning one), for which there is an overload of anything which you can overload in c++.
You can instantiate a wrapper from some c++ value, in which case the wrapper will just forward everything to this value, which was nice for debugging in the preagentic era.
But, you can also instantiate such a wrapper as a tracer, and the result of the functions evaluation will be a trace.
For controlflow, we record whenever a wrapper type is evaluated as a bool, first return true, and when we reach the end of one branch, throw an exception to get back to the beginning, and start all over again, but evaluate it to false.
The resulting trace we can turn into LLVM IR and compile, or run for example in wasm

Pick a random cell for modification, based on its "energy" (higher energy get modified first):
1. Every conflicting cell gets energy +1.0 (try to resolve conflicts before new empty cells).  E.g. two 7s on the same row both get +1 energy.
2. Empty cells have small energy 0.1
3. Filled cells with no conflicts have energy 0
For the selected cell, choose a digit.  Look at numbers in its row/column, every occurrence of a number in the row/col drop prob of sampling by 90%.  Example:
| No. of 7s | chance of 7 |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 10% (equal to other digits) |
| 1 | 1% |
| 2 | 0.1% |
Obviously this would get more complex with more numbers on the line (this is just checking 7 on otherwise empty line).
This is essentially what these models are doing.  It provides a kind of "wave function collapse" search with random exploration based on "energy", but energy is just defined as conflict / unsolved.  For something like a maze, energy is disconnected path segments or walls, etc.
